resources.string: Each system installs separately and keeps its own files. Switching only changes which one the main screen installs and launches — nothing already installed is removed.
This deletes the whole system — about %1$s — including every program and file inside it. It cannot be undone; reinstalling means downloading it again.
Installed systems use %1$s · %2$s free on this device
The system could not be downloaded or unpacked. This usually means the network dropped, or the device ran out of space.
The desktop could not be installed. The package downloads may have failed part-way.
The desktop did not start. The log has the reason.
Desktop is up at %1$s — install a VNC viewer to connect.
Type a command, e.g. apt list --installed
The session log has been added to the console below.
Installed when this system was still offered. It can only be removed now.
Could not reconnect to the desktop: %1$s. The session may still be running — close this view and launch again.
The X server left no message at all, which usually means it was killed rather than that it crashed — on a phone that is the system reclaiming memory.
Could not start it again. Go back and look at the log.
The X server crashed — its own error is in the log below.

The X server left no error behind, so it did not crash: something killed it. On a phone that is almost always the system reclaiming memory, and it happens under heavy work — a package upgrade, or a video playing.

The log contains a read that failed with \"Function not implemented\", which cannot happen on a healthy system: it is what the kernel does when the process tracing the container has gone. So the session did not fail on its own — the floor was taken out from under it, and the thing to explain is why proot was killed, not why the desktop crashed.

Free memory while the session was running, oldest first:
%1$s

If it was falling towards zero, memory is the answer. If it was not, something else ended the session and memory is not the explanation.

The always-on service runs from inside this system:

%1$s

Its working files go with it. If they include an identity or a key, reinstalling will not bring it back — whatever used it will come back as something new.
That rules memory out. The least free at any point was %1$s, and Android never called the device low — so nothing was killed to reclaim space, and the cause is elsewhere.
it exited normally, which means it was asked to stop rather than killed.
killed by signal %1$d (SIGKILL) — that comes from outside the process. On a phone it is Android reclaiming, or a power manager ending the app\'s work.
killed by signal %1$d (SIGSYS) — the sandbox refused a system call that proot itself made. Nothing inside the container can prevent that; it is Android\'s seccomp filter.
killed by signal %1$d — proot failed on its own account, which is a bug in it rather than anything the desktop did.
stopped by signal %1$d (SIGTERM) — something asked it to end.

Processes running inside the system: %1$d at the last reading, %2$d at the most. Android allows an app 32 processes outside its own management, counted across all apps, and kills them when that is passed — so a number near or above 32 is the explanation, and a number well below it means the cause is something else again.

Busiest reading: the system used %1$d%% of one processor core, and proot itself %2$d%%. Android\'s limit on an app\'s unmanaged processes covers processor use as well as number, under the same switch — and proot is the process it kills, so its figure is the one that matters.

One command, kept running inside the system — a relay, a server, a bot. It is started again if it stops, it survives closing the desktop and leaving the app, and it comes back after the device reboots.
Switched on, but nothing is running yet.
Enter a command first — there is nothing to run.
Allow it to run in the background
Android is still allowed to put this app to sleep, which pauses the service for hours at a time. Granting the exemption is what makes \"always on\" true.
Android is allowed to keep it running in the background.
